item.text: {"text":"Ranking against 99 negatives can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog ranking—even in expectation; repeated sampling does not eliminate this bias ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). A [RecSys 2025 study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) further distinguishes sampling resolution, fidelity, robustness to exposure bias, and predictive power. For this task, pinned macro validation HR@10 remains the selection objective. Full-catalog diagnostics measure a different property; neither their improvement nor lower training loss establishes improvement on that objective. Popularity slices are useful: a [2024 reproduction](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/33989) found popularity-bias conclusions sensitive to datasets, algorithms, user grouping, and evaluation strategy.\n\nProposed calibration: measure whether probe changes track validation HR@10 changes across checkpoints and trials, reporting each category alongside the equal-weight macro average. Use training-derived popularity and history-length slices, with counts. Training-only chronological replay can probe next-item behavior, but a model already trained on replay targets yields an in-sample diagnostic; credible temporal evaluation requires withholding those targets and excluding future information from fitting and statistics. [RecSys 2025 temporal-splitting research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748164) documents global-timeline leakage risks. For uncertainty, resample paired user-level hit differences within each category, then average the four category differences equally; this estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fixed candidates and trained models, not training-seed variability or repeated-search bias. Keep the twenty users’ full-catalog lists explicitly qualitative: report unseen-item filtering, popularity concentration, coverage, and title-based observations without inferring satisfaction, simulator traits, or validation accuracy."}
